cells.tense: You're here, carrying, and still open.
cells.verb: letting things reach you before you know what they are
cells.place: in the part of you that bears weight without going hard
cells.ask: let one thing in past the point where you think you've understood the load — what comes back is a knowing that keeps deepening instead of closing.
cells.core:
You're here, carrying, and still open. The weight hasn't shut the door — you can be reached while you hold, which most people can't do; they pick one. Something lands on you and you feel it arrive, and the carrying goes on anyway. That's not two things. That's one strength wearing both faces.

If this balance wants somewhere to go, it isn't toward holding more. It's toward letting one thing reach you past the point where you'd normally say "I've got the shape of it." What comes back is a kind of knowing that doesn't finish — it just keeps getting truer.
cells.sheetLine: You can be reached while you carry, and the carrying holds.

cells.tense: You're bracing open for everything that might land.
cells.verb: taking in every weight before it's even yours
cells.place: in the part of you that's supposed to hold its shape under pressure
cells.ask: choose one thing to carry all the way to finished, by your own decision, and let that completed shape be what holds you — what comes back is openness you can afford, because something in you has edges again.
cells.core:
You're bracing open for everything that might land. Not just what's here — what's coming, what might come, what someone might feel next week. The door isn't open; it's been taken off the hinges. And the part of you built to hold under pressure can't hold when nothing has a shape, so it's flooding instead of standing.

The way back isn't to feel less. It's to pick one thing — one — and carry it through to done, because you decided to, not because it was pressing on you. A finished thing has edges. Edges are what make openness survivable.
cells.sheetLine: You're open to weight that hasn't even arrived yet.

cells.tense: Somewhere back there you closed, and it held.
cells.verb: no longer letting anything new reach you
cells.place: in the part of you that keeps going under weight
cells.ask: instead of trying to feel, take something you once set out to do and carry it the rest of the way as if you'd never touched it before — what comes back is a heart that opens on its own because you're actually here again.
cells.core:
Somewhere back there you closed, and it held. Letting things reach you made the carrying harder, so you stopped being reachable — and the load didn't fall. You're still standing. You're just standing with the door shut, and the door has been shut long enough that you've started calling it a wall.

Don't try to pry it open; forcing feeling into a closed place only proves it should stay closed. Go sideways. Take something you once meant to do and carry it the rest of the way, fresh, like the first time you held it. Being that present to one thing pulls the whole of you back into the room — and the door opens because you're on this side of it again.
cells.sheetLine: You shut the door to keep carrying, and now you're only carrying.

cells.tense: Things are reaching you right now, and you're not calling it that.
cells.verb: being touched by what you carry
cells.place: in the part of you that just keeps bearing it
cells.ask: say "that got to me" about one thing, without explaining or defending it — what comes back is knowing you can trust, with room in it for not knowing yet.
cells.core:
Things are reaching you right now, and you're not calling it that. The weight gets through — it changes how you stand, what you set down first, who you go quiet around — and when asked you'd say you're just getting on with it. The openness is doing real work. It's just working under someone else's name.

The way back is smaller than it sounds. One thing, once: "that got to me." No reason attached, no case made for why it counted. You already know it landed; the knowing came before the words did. Let it stand without proof, and you'll find you can trust it — and trust the not-knowing-yet that comes with it.
cells.sheetLine: It's getting through to you. You call it getting on with it.
